title: The Puzzle of the Pyramid
summary: On a school trip to Egypt, a curious student works with a real archaeologist to decode hieroglyphic inscriptions and learns historical facts about how the pyramids were built and what ancient Egyptians believed.
poll: Ancient Egyptian beliefs about gods are too strange for modern students to learn about.

versions.title: The Puzzle of the Pyramid
versions.text:
Mona went on a trip to Egypt. She went with her class.

Mona met a woman named Hana. Hana looks at old things.

They stood by a big, ancient pyramid. It was very old. It was made of big stone blocks.

Hana showed Mona a flat stone. The stone had small marks on it. Each mark was a sign. Old folks wrote with signs like this.

"Can you read the signs?" Mona asked.

"Yes," said Hana. "This one means bird. This one means water."

"How did men build the pyramid?" Mona asked.

"Long ago, men cut big blocks," said Hana. "They moved the blocks up ramps. Many men worked for years."

"What did old folks think back then?" Mona asked.

"They thought there were many gods," said Hana. "That was part of what they thought. It helps us learn about their history."

Mona wrote facts in her book. She wanted to learn more signs. She loved to help with this work.

versions.title: The Puzzle of the Pyramid

Mona went on a school trip to Egypt with her class, and she was thrilled to finally see the pyramids she had read about.

Mona met a woman named Dr. Hana, who studies old things for a living and had worked at this site for many years. Dr. Hana was friendly and clearly loved explaining her work to visitors.

They stood beside a huge, ancient pyramid built from giant blocks of stone. Mona could hardly believe how massive and old it really was.

Dr. Hana showed Mona a flat stone covered with small, careful marks. Each mark was a sign, and old Egyptians used signs like these to write words long ago, instead of letters like ours.

"Can you actually read these signs?" Mona asked curiously.

"Yes," said Dr. Hana. "This sign means bird. This one means water. Put together, these two signs can make a whole word."

"How did people manage to build something this huge?" Mona asked.

"Long ago, many workers cut huge blocks of stone from quarries," Dr. Hana explained. "They moved the heavy blocks up long ramps using ropes. Thousands of workers worked together for many years to finish it."

"What did the old Egyptians believe about the world?" Mona asked.

"They believed in many different gods," said Dr. Hana. "That belief was part of their daily lives and their stories. We study it today to learn about their history, not because we believe it ourselves."

Mona carefully wrote the facts down in her notebook. She wanted to learn even more signs before the trip ended. She loved helping with this kind of careful work.

versions.title: The Puzzle of the Pyramid
versions.text:
Mona traveled to Egypt on a school trip with her class, thrilled to finally see the pyramids she had only read about.

On the trip, Mona met an archaeologist named Dr. Hana, who had studied ancient Egypt for many years and worked at a few excavation sites. Dr. Hana clearly loved explaining her discoveries to curious visitors.

They stood beside a huge, ancient pyramid built from enormous blocks of stone. Mona could hardly believe how massive the structure really was.

Dr. Hana showed Mona a flat stone covered with careful, tiny carvings. Each carving was a hieroglyph, a picture-sign ancient Egyptians used to write words, long before modern alphabets existed.

"Can you read these hieroglyphs?" Mona asked curiously.

"Yes," said Dr. Hana. "This sign represents a bird. This one represents water. Together, these signs can form a word."

"How did people manage to build something this big?" Mona wondered aloud.

"Long ago, thousands of workers cut massive blocks of stone from distant quarries," Dr. Hana explained. "They dragged the blocks up long ramps using ropes and simple tools. It took many years of teamwork to finish such a project."

"What did the ancient Egyptians believe about the world?" Mona asked.

"They believed in many gods, who they thought controlled nature and the afterlife," said Dr. Hana. "That belief shaped their daily lives and their stories. Today, we study it as history, not as something we believe ourselves."

Mona carefully recorded these facts in her notebook. She wanted to learn even more hieroglyphs before the trip ended. She loved helping with this kind of careful work.

"Yes," said Dr. Hana. "This sign represents a bird. This one represents water. Put together in a certain order, these signs can form an entire word."

"Long ago, thousands of workers cut massive blocks of stone from distant quarries," Dr. Hana explained patiently. "They dragged the heavy blocks up long ramps using ropes and simple tools. It took many years of careful teamwork to finish such an enormous project."

"They believed in many different gods, who they thought controlled nature, the sky, and even the afterlife," said Dr. Hana. "That belief shaped their daily lives, their art, and their stories. Today, we study it carefully as history, not as something we believe ourselves."

versions.title: The Puzzle of the Pyramid
versions.text:
Mona traveled to Egypt on a school trip with her class, thrilled to finally witness in person the pyramids she had only read about in books and photographs.

On the trip, Mona was introduced to an archaeologist named Dr. Hana, who had devoted many years to studying ancient Egypt. Dr. Hana had worked on several notable excavations scattered across the country, carefully uncovering artifacts that few outsiders had ever examined up close.

They stood together beside a colossal, ancient pyramid built from enormous blocks of stone. Each block towered far above Mona's own height, arranged with a precision that still puzzled modern engineers who studied it.

Dr. Hana showed Mona a flat stone covered with careful, precise carvings arranged in neat rows across its weathered surface. Each carving was a hieroglyph, a picture-sign that ancient Egyptians had used to record words and ideas, long before modern alphabets existed.

When Mona asked whether anyone could still read these ancient signs, Dr. Hana explained that scholars had learned to recognize many of them. A bird-shaped sign and a water-shaped sign, she said, could be combined in a specific order to form an entire word, almost like solving a puzzle left behind by people long dead. Mona wondered how scholars could be sure they had correctly decoded the meaning of an inscription rather than simply guessing.

Curious about the pyramid itself, Mona wondered aloud how anyone could have built something this enormous without modern machinery. Dr. Hana explained that thousands of laborers had once quarried massive blocks of stone from distant sites, dragging the heavy blocks up long ramps using ropes and simple wooden tools, a task that required many years of coordinated teamwork.

When Mona finally asked what the ancient Egyptians had believed about the world around them, Dr. Hana explained that they had believed in numerous different gods, whom they thought governed nature, the sky, and the afterlife awaiting everyone after death. That belief had shaped their daily lives, their artwork, and the stories passed down through generations, and modern scholars now study it carefully as history rather than as something they themselves believe.

Mona carefully recorded these fascinating facts in her notebook, determined not to overlook a single detail from such a remarkable day. She silently hoped to decipher even more hieroglyphs before the trip ended, having genuinely come to love this kind of careful, scientific work.

options: To make Mona believe in old gods and spirits
To help Mona build a brand new pyramid someday
To learn about their history, not to believe it
To teach Mona ancient Egyptian magic spells and tricks
questions.why: Dr. Hana studies old beliefs as part of history, to understand the past, not because she believes those old ideas herself.

wrong.A: Dr. Hana does not try to make Mona believe in old gods.
wrong.B: Dr. Hana studies the pyramid; she does not build a new one.
wrong.D: Nothing in the story is about magic.

questions.stem: Why does the author have Dr. Hana explain her work to Mona?
options: To show that Mona is a poor listener in the class
To help readers learn facts about Egypt the way Mona does
To make the story longer for the readers to enjoy
To show that archaeologists are right about the past
questions.why: Dr. Hana's explanations let readers learn the same facts about pyramids and signs that Mona is learning.

wrong.A: Mona listens closely and asks good questions.
wrong.C: The explanations teach facts; they do not just add length.
wrong.D: The story never claims archaeologists are always right.

LOW.prompt: Would you like to work with an archaeologist like Dr. Hana? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.

keyWords.definition: a picture-sign used by ancient Egyptians to write words
keyWords.example: The hieroglyph of a bird appeared on the temple wall.

keyWords.definition: a scientist who studies old objects and places to learn about the past
keyWords.example: The archaeologist carefully dug up an old clay pot.

keyWords.definition: to find something that was not known before
keyWords.example: Scientists discovered an old coin buried in the sand.

keyWords.definition: a picture or shape cut into a hard material like stone or wood
keyWords.example: The carving on the temple wall showed a river.

keyWords.definition: the careful digging of a site to find old objects or buildings
keyWords.example: The team began an excavation near the old city walls.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Mona learns how archaeologists use hieroglyphs, construction methods, and historical beliefs to understand ancient Egypt, as part of real scientific study.
Mona discovers hidden treasure buried beneath the pyramid, and she keeps the gold and jewels for herself and her family.
Mona becomes an expert at building pyramids herself, and the story ends when she finishes her own tall tomb of stone.
Mona proves that ancient Egyptian gods still exist today, and she speaks with them inside the temple during the night, to the surprise of her class.
questions.why: The story centers on Mona learning, as real history and science, how hieroglyphs, construction, and old beliefs help us understand ancient Egypt.

wrong.B: No treasure is discovered in the story.
wrong.C: Mona learns about building methods; she does not become a builder herself.
wrong.D: The story treats old gods as history, not as something real today.

questions.stem: What is a hieroglyph, according to Dr. Hana?
options: A tool used to cut stone blocks in the quarry
A picture-sign ancient Egyptians used to write words
A type of ramp used to move heavy stones up the side
A kind of pyramid found only in Egypt
questions.why: Dr. Hana explains that a hieroglyph is a picture-sign that ancient Egyptians used to write words.

wrong.A: Cutting tools are not called hieroglyphs in the story.
wrong.C: Ramps are used for moving stones, not for writing.
wrong.D: A hieroglyph is a sign, not a type of pyramid.

questions.stem: How did workers move the heavy stone blocks up the pyramid?
options: They carried each block by hand
They used modern trucks
They used ramps and ropes
They rolled the blocks down a hill
questions.why: Dr. Hana explains that workers dragged the heavy blocks up ramps using ropes and simple tools.

wrong.A: The blocks were far too heavy to carry by hand.
wrong.B: No trucks existed in ancient Egypt.
wrong.D: The blocks were moved up the pyramid, not down a hill.

questions.stem: In the story, the word archaeologist means —
options: a person who builds new buildings with bricks and glass
a person who guides tourists around a city and tells jokes
a person who writes modern books for children and adults
a person who studies old things and places from the past
questions.why: Dr. Hana is an archaeologist, someone who studies old objects and places to learn about history.

wrong.A: An archaeologist studies old buildings; she does not construct new ones.
wrong.B: Dr. Hana studies ancient Egypt; she is not described as a tour guide.
wrong.C: The story is not about writing modern books.

questions.stem: Why does Dr. Hana say they study ancient beliefs as history rather than as something they believe themselves?
options: Because studying the past does not mean accepting its beliefs as true today
Because ancient Egyptians still worship those gods today
Because the story says modern Egyptians agree with these old beliefs about the gods
Because the gods described are scientifically proven to be real
questions.why: Dr. Hana's explanation shows that learning about a belief from the past is different from believing it is true now.

wrong.B: The story describes this as an old, historical belief, not a current practice.
wrong.C: The story never claims modern people agree with these beliefs.
wrong.D: No proof of the gods' existence is claimed anywhere in the story.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why building the pyramid took so many years?
options: The work required an enormous number of workers moving stones one at a time
The workers took long breaks every single day, so the building was slow and the king grew tired
The pyramid was rebuilt many times after collapsing, so it took many years to finish the blocks
One worker was allowed to build at a time, so each stone had to wait in a long line
questions.why: Moving thousands of massive stone blocks with ramps and ropes, rather than machines, naturally required years of steady work by many people.

wrong.B: The story does not mention long breaks causing delays.
wrong.C: No collapse or rebuilding is mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: The story describes thousands of workers, not just one.

questions.stem: What allows scholars today to understand what some hieroglyphs mean?
options: Guessing randomly until something sounds right to the scholars
Comparing signs that repeat across many different carvings
Asking modern Egyptians to translate them directly
Reading a dictionary written by ancient Egyptians
questions.why: Dr. Hana explains that comparing symbols that recur across many monuments helps reveal their likely meaning.

wrong.A: The story describes careful comparison, not random guessing.
wrong.C: No modern translators are mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: No ancient dictionary is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: How does the story mainly present information about ancient Egypt?
options: Through a list of facts with no characters
Through a conversation between a curious student and an archaeologist
Through a diary written by an ancient Egyptian
Through a long and detailed comparison between ancient Egypt and another distant country
questions.why: The story presents facts through Mona's questions and Dr. Hana's answers as they examine the pyramid together.

wrong.A: The story has clear characters, Mona and Dr. Hana.
wrong.C: No diary appears in the story.
wrong.D: The story never compares Egypt to another country.

MID.prompt: Explain how archaeologists like Dr. Hana learn facts about ancient Egypt. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how archaeologists learn facts about the past.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.

keyWords.definition: an object made by people in the past that tells us about their lives
keyWords.example: The museum displayed a bronze artifact from an old shipwreck.

keyWords.definition: a life some people believe continues after a person dies
keyWords.example: Many ancient cultures had their own ideas about the afterlife.

keyWords.definition: to figure out the meaning of a message written in signs or symbols
keyWords.example: The team worked for months to decode the old message.

keyWords.definition: words or symbols carved into a hard surface such as stone or metal
keyWords.example: An inscription on the old coin gave the date it was made.

keyWords.definition: belonging to a time very far in the past, long before recent history
keyWords.example: The explorers found an ancient map hidden deep in a cave.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: Archaeological study of inscriptions, construction techniques, and ancient beliefs allows scholars to reconstruct history without endorsing beliefs they themselves do not hold.

Ancient Egyptian gods directly intervened to help build the pyramids, as the inscriptions say, and so Dr. Hana teaches that they are real and active in the modern world, and she asks her students to agree.
Mona proves that modern engineers could never match ancient building methods, and Dr. Hana agrees that no one today can ever build such pyramids.
Dr. Hana secretly believes that the gods described in the inscriptions are real, and she tells the class to pray to them.
questions.why: The story's central idea is that careful archaeological study, of writing, building methods, and belief systems, lets scholars understand history without accepting old beliefs as true.

wrong.B: The story never suggests gods actually acted in building the pyramid; it describes human labor.
wrong.C: No such comparison to modern engineers appears in the story.
wrong.D: Dr. Hana clearly frames the gods as historical belief, not something she personally believes.

questions.stem: According to Dr. Hana, how do scholars decode the meaning of unfamiliar hieroglyphs?
options: By translating them instantly using a modern dictionary of the old words
By asking current religious leaders what the symbols mean to them
By comparing symbols that recur across numerous inscriptions and monuments
By guessing based on how the symbols look to the eye
questions.why: Dr. Hana explains that scholars compare recurring symbols across many monuments and documents to work out their likely meaning.

wrong.A: No modern dictionary of ancient Egyptian existed when this writing was first used.
wrong.B: No religious leaders are consulted in the story.
wrong.D: The story describes careful comparison, not simple guessing based on appearance.

questions.stem: What specific method did ancient laborers use to move massive stone blocks?
options: Floating the blocks downstream on rafts
Lifting the blocks with early machines resembling modern cranes
Carrying the blocks individually on their shoulders
Dragging the blocks up long ramps using ropes and simple tools
questions.why: Dr. Hana explains that laborers dragged heavy blocks up long ramps with ropes and simple wooden tools.

wrong.A: No rafts or rivers are mentioned for moving the stones.
wrong.B: No cranes or similar machines are described in the story.
wrong.C: The blocks were far too heavy for a single worker to carry alone.

questions.stem: In the story, the word afterlife most nearly refers to —
options: a type of ancient Egyptian currency
a form of life believed to continue after death
a season in the ancient Egyptian calendar for farming
a region located south of ancient Egypt
questions.why: The story describes the afterlife as something ancient Egyptians believed waited for people after death.

wrong.A: Afterlife is not a kind of money.
wrong.C: Afterlife is not described as a season.
wrong.D: Afterlife is not a place located south of Egypt.

questions.stem: Why does Dr. Hana treat ancient Egyptian religious beliefs as a subject of historical study rather than as truths to accept?
options: Because the ancient Egyptians themselves no longer practice their old religion
Because modern science has proven every ancient Egyptian belief false
Because the Egyptian government requires archaeologists to disbelieve it
Because studying what a civilization believed does not require sharing that belief
questions.why: Dr. Hana's approach shows that understanding a past civilization's beliefs as history does not mean an archaeologist must personally accept them as true.

wrong.A: The story does not discuss whether anyone practices the old religion today.
wrong.B: The story never claims science has disproven these beliefs.
wrong.C: No government requirement is mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about the reliability of a single, uncompared guess at a hieroglyph's meaning?
options: A single guess could be mistaken and mislead other scholars for years
A single guess is accurate, so nobody needs to check it later
A single guess is official once an archaeologist states it in public
A single guess requires no further checking by other scholars
questions.why: Dr. Hana explains that a mistaken guess, without careful comparison, could mislead an entire field of study for decades.

wrong.B: The story warns that an uncompared guess could easily be wrong.
wrong.C: The story emphasizes careful checking, not simply declaring a guess official.
wrong.D: The story stresses that guesses require extensive checking.

questions.stem: What was the ultimate cause of the pyramid's immense scale, according to Dr. Hana's explanation?
options: A single wealthy ruler personally lifting each stone by himself
Supernatural forces moving the stones overnight while workers slept
Many thousands of coordinated workers laboring together for years
Modern machinery secretly used in ancient times by the builders
questions.why: Dr. Hana attributes the pyramid's massive scale to the coordinated labor of thousands of workers over many years.

wrong.A: No single ruler is described lifting stones alone.
wrong.B: The story explains human labor, not supernatural forces.
wrong.D: No modern machinery is described as being used in ancient times.

questions.stem: Why does the author have Mona ask how scholars can be certain about a hieroglyph's meaning?
options: To suggest that archaeology is really just random guessing by scholars with old books
To show that careful, evidence-based methods, not guesswork, are behind historical knowledge
To prove that ancient Egyptian writing cannot be understood by anyone
To criticize Dr. Hana for her weak and boring teaching methods in the lab
questions.why: Mona's question lets Dr. Hana explain that patient, careful comparison, not guessing, is what makes historical knowledge reliable.

wrong.A: Dr. Hana's answer shows the opposite: careful method, not guessing.
wrong.C: The story shows hieroglyphs CAN be understood through careful study.
wrong.D: The question is curious, not critical of Dr. Hana.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says ancient Egyptian beliefs about gods are too strange for modern students to learn about. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about history, archaeology, and ancient beliefs.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.

Pieces of wood
Big stone blocks
Sheets of metal

very new
very small

wrong.C: The pyramid is big, not small.

wrong.D: Boats are not mentioned.

MID.stem: Where did the workers cut the huge stone blocks?
options: From distant quarries
From the nearby river
From the sea floor
From the pyramid's top

wrong.C: The sea floor is not mentioned.

very old
very large
very bright

wrong.A: Massive is the opposite of light.
wrong.B: Old is a different idea from massive.
wrong.D: Brightness is not the point.

MID.stem: What does Mona's notebook show about her?
options: She wants to draw maps
She is eager to learn
She dislikes the trip
She is too shy to talk

wrong.C: She is thrilled about the trip.
wrong.D: She asks many questions.

options: She got to meet a king
She was going to win a prize
She was done with school
She could see the pyramids

wrong.B: No prize is in the story.

HIGH.stem: According to Dr. Hana, how can a bird sign and a water sign form a word?
options: They are spoken aloud
They are drawn smaller
They are put in a set order
They are written in red ink

wrong.D: Ink color is not mentioned.

options: tiny
gigantic
ordinary
fragile

wrong.C: The pyramid is not ordinary.
wrong.D: A pyramid of stone is not fragile.

HIGH.stem: Why does the author compare reading hieroglyphs to solving a puzzle?
options: To show that signs must be pieced together
To say the signs are a game for children
To show that no one can read them
To say the stone was found in a box
HIGH.why: Like puzzle pieces, the signs must be combined in the right order to make meaning.

wrong.B: The text treats the work as serious science.
wrong.C: The text says scholars can read many signs.

options: Through a list of dates
Through a long speech by Mona
Through a diary kept by Dr. Hana
Through questions and answers
HIGH.why: Mona keeps asking questions, and Dr. Hana answers each one in turn.
